title: Normalizing Flow Maps

paper.title: Normalizing Flow Maps
paper.abstract:
Abstract Scalable approaches to learning neural dynamical systems have placed diffusion, flow matching, and few-step generators in flow maps at the forefront of generative modeling. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps ( NFM ), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFM s learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction.
To enable scalable training of NFM s, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFM s that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process.
On conditional image generation on CIFAR- 10 10 and ImageNet- 64 64 , NFM s achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFM s outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Learning a transport map between a tractable reference distribution and the empirical distribution of complex data has become the de facto paradigm in generative modeling, with varied application domains spanning audiovisual media ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) , biomolecular modeling ( Abramson et al., 2024 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) , and scientific simulation ( Shu et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ) . Driving this widespread adoption is the ability to leverage standard alignment techniques such as best-of- N N selection ( Ramesh et al., 2021 ) , inference-time steering ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , and post-training algorithms ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) which effectively sharpen the model distribution—by increasing sample rewards assessed by an oracle. However, each generated sample necessitates computationally expensive numerical integration of an ODE or SDE—producing a substantial inference tax that computationally challenges the steering and post-training pipeline ( Wohlwend et al., 2025 ; Scarpellini et al., 2026 ) . Indeed, while typical Autoregressive LLMs have a mature post-training stack—e.g., PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , etc.—corresponding algorithmic frameworks for diffusion and flow model post-training are both vast and varied ( Wallace et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . The crucial distinction is that LLMs natively provide tractable sample likelihoods, whereas evaluating exact densities for diffusion and flow-matching models is computationally challenging. Specifically, evaluating sample likelihoods of flow models requires integrating the instantaneous change of variables along the underlying ODE, computing a high-dimensional network Jacobian, and necessitates stochastic trace estimation ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Meyer et al., 2021 ) . Instead, it is computationally more attractive to target the reward-tilted distribution, by modifying the drift of the underlying dynamics through path-space objectives. These objectives, however, crucially rely on high-variance value estimates of the terminal reward. More precisely, value function estimation necessitates propagating terminal rewards through noisy intermediate states, which requires backpropagating through time ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) –or a noisy single-step denoising approximation ( Blasingame and Liu, 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026b ) . These algorithmic features combine and give rise to tilting objectives that are inherently high variance, often leading to unstable post-training and mode collapse. Figure 1: Overview of NFM , which performs generative transport along a stochastic interpolant. NFM-R exploits pointwise matching at the particle level, while NFM-D leverages distributional matching. As generative models are deployed at scale, the cumulative cost of repeated sampling for generation, steering, and post-training makes inference efficiency a central design consideration. This practical motivation has led to the emergence of flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2025b ) , that directly learn the flow integrator , effectively compressing numerical simulation into few network evaluations. Although the exact ODE flow is a diffeomorphism, standard parameterizations are not invertible, nor do they provide tractable Jacobian determinants. While flow maps reduce the inference tax, they do not resolve the crucial likelihood-access gap—limiting their usage in scientific applications like Boltzmann Generators ( Noé et al., 2019 ) . As a result, classical Normalizing Flows (NF) ( Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010 ; Tabak and Turner, 2013 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ; Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ) trained with MLE remain an attractive exact likelihood-based model class. However, their practical deployment critically relies on noise injection into the clean data distribution for stable training, which unfortunately eliminates the promised access to cheap sample likelihood ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Taken together, these considerations motivate a new generative model that combines few-step sampling of flow maps with exact sample likelihoods for scalable, likelihood-based post-training. Current work . In this paper, we introduce Normalizing Flow Maps ( NFM ), a new generative model family, depicted in fig. 1 , that is purpose-built to deliver two objectives of interest: 1.) Exact sample likelihoods and 2.) Few-step inference ; thereby generalizing classical invertible normalizing flows and endowing flow maps with tractable likelihoods. An NFM defines a time-conditioned generative transport operator that is tied to the law of a known stochastic interpolant. However, unlike existing model classes, NFM by construction defines a family of tractable invertible maps connecting arbitrary points along a prescribed probability path. Consequently, NFM s provide exact sample likelihoods without expensive numerical integration. Importantly, restricting this family to the prior and data endpoints recovers a normalizing flow, and querying arbitrary time pairs yields the few-step transport characteristics of a flow map. As a result, NFM s are naturally suited for applications that require sample likelihoods, such as Boltzmann generators ( Noé et al., 2019 ) and RLHF post-training. To train NFM s, we operationalize two complementary matching principles inherent to NFM s, which in turn lead to self-distillation training objectives. In particular, our key insight is that NFM s must satisfy a known stochastic interpolant at a pointwise level and/or match its marginal distribution . The former condition unlocks regression-based training common in flow maps, but adapted to NFM , while the latter is an altogether new algorithmic framework that trains few-step generators by exploiting NFM s family of (end-point) invertible maps. We summarize our main contributions: 1. Model class . We introduce NFM , a new generative model class, that learns an invertible pushforward map, while natively supporting few-step sampling and exact sample likelihoods. 2. Training algorithms . Defined by matching principles (§ 3.2 ), we design two instantiations in NFM-R and NFM-D , which leverages pointwise and distributional matching respectively. In particular, NFM-R optimizes ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regression objectives. Meanwhile, NFM-D matches the induced pushforward distributions along the marginal law of the known forward process. 3. Empirical analysis . We evaluate NFM across image generation, post-training, and equilibrium sampling. On CIFAR- 10 10 and ImageNet- 64 64 , NFM improves over MLE-trained NFs in FID and FLD while for BGs NFM improves over prior continuous flow approaches. We also demonstrate that exact tractable likelihoods of NFM enable direct post-training unlike diffusion models.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We introduce Normalizing Flow Maps ( NFM ), a new generative model class built from two-time pushforward maps that learn generative transport along the probability path of a stochastic interpolant. More precisely, NFM s generalize classical normalizing flows across time, combining the large transport-step capabilities of jump operators while endowing previous flow maps with tractable inverses that enable exact sample likelihoods, i.e., p 0 ​ ( x 0 ) p_{0}(x_{0}) . We first define the model and its parameterizations (§ 3.1 ), then expose the inherent computational properties at the particle and distributional level. These principles yield (self)-distillation objectives (§ 3.3 ) resulting in NFM-R that is constructed from pointwise matching of the probability flow and NFM-D that leverages distributional matching of its marginals. Finally, we demonstrate RLHF-based post-training in § 3.4 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Pointwise and Distributional Matching
sections.text: An NFM describes generative transport with respect to a target stochastic interpolant, through both its action on particles and its induced pushforward density. At optimality, the particle and distributional perspectives must be consistent in describing the same stochastic interpolant, yielding two complementary matching laws that describe transport along an NFM . We now develop these pointwise and distributional matching principles which, in turn, result in self-distillation losses in § 3.3 . Pointwise matching laws . At the particle level, an NFM resembles a conventional flow map operator and jumps along the stochastic interpolant I t I_{t} , with a target conditional velocity field, v t ∗ ​ ( x t | x 0 , x 1 ) v^{*}_{t}(x_{t}|x_{0},x_{1}) , as defined in Equation 2 . sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We empirically validate NFM on image generation and RL post-training, as well as on a variety of molecular conformation sampling tasks. We use the denoiser parametrization (B) for NFM-R , the dual-time parametrization (A) for one-step NFM-D and gated dual-time parametrization (C) for few-step NFM-D (§ 3.1 ). Both methods use iTARFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) as the base invertible architecture Φ s , t θ \Phi_{s,t}^{\theta} (see § D.2 ), which also serves as our principal baseline when trained with MLE. Additional ablations and experimental details are reported in § E .

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Normalizing flows . NFs ( Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010 ; Tabak and Turner, 2013 ; Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ) are invertible generative models whose exact likelihood can be evaluated via the change-of-variables formula. Despite this appealing property, scaling to tasks like image generation remains challenging due to numerical instabilities ( Xu and Campbell, 2023 ; Andrade, 2024 ) and architectural constraints ( Chen et al., 2019 ) . Recently, TARFlows ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in image ( Gu et al., 2026a ; Shen et al., 2026 ) and video generation ( Gu et al., 2026c ) , as well as in sampling from Boltzmann distributions ( Midgley et al., 2023 ; Tan et al., 2025a ; Tan et al., 2025b ) . While TARFlow is trained via noise augmented MLE ( Loaiza-Ganem et al., 2023 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) , alternative training strategies include training over a probability path ( Kim et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2026b ) , and direct regression-based training ( Rehman et al., 2026b ) . Stochastic interpolants and flow maps . Diffusion ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) and Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) models have achieved state-of-the-art sample fidelity across numerous modalities ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Abramson et al., 2024 ; Zeni et al., 2025 ) . Generating samples and evaluating likelihoods with these models typically require costly numerical integration ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Grathwohl et al., 2018 ) , motivating the development of few-step models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) , and the flow map framework ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Boffi et al., 2025b ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) . While flow maps accelerate sampling, likelihood evaluation remains costly ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) . Alternatively, proxy likelihood evaluation can be amortized using an auxiliary divergence predictor ( Ai et al., 2026 ; OuYang et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we introduce Normalizing Flow Maps , a family of invertible transport maps that combine few-step sampling with exact change-of-variables densities for one-step endpoint samples. We demonstrate the application of these cheap likelihoods in Boltzmann generators through importance sampling, and straightforward RL-based post-training of image generation models. Furthermore, we demonstrate superior sample quality to existing NF methods and avoid the use of Tweedie denoising which requires spatial gradients and breaks invertibility guarantees. While NFM-R obtains the highest sample quality, it is prone to becoming numerically non-invertible, which impedes RL methods relying on the score-function or KL-regularization. This points to the importance of designing training schemes that enjoy the benefits of both pointwise and distributional consistency.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Our method is a general purpose generative modeling approach. In the image experiments, we post-train class-conditional generators using text–to–image reward models. These rewards are imperfect proxies for human preferences: optimizing them may amplify biases in the reward models or favor images that score well without matching a user’s intent. In the molecular experiments, we evaluate equilibrium conformation sampling on existing peptide benchmarks using molecular dynamics data. The molecules studied in this work are considered safe and non-toxic. Applying the method to other molecular systems would require evaluation specific to those uses.

Appendix B Exact likelihood without Tweedie denoising
sections.text: In Figure 5 , we compare guided MNIST samples from an iTARFlow trained via MLE without additive Gaussian noise and an iTARFlow trained with Gaussian noise augmentation and Tweedie denoising at inference time. In this experiment, training without noise produces visibly poor samples, despite retaining the flow’s exact invertibility condition. Noise augmentation followed by denoising substantially improves sample quality. However, the flow’s tractable density describes its outputs before denoising. The subsequent Tweedie transformation is not guaranteed to be invertible, and its Jacobian determinant is not accounted for by the flow’s likelihood calculation. Consequently, the likelihood of the denoised output distribution is not provided by the original flow. This comparison illustrates the practical difficulty, in our setting, of obtaining both high-quality samples and tractable exact likelihoods for the same output distribution. (a) MLE without noise. (b) MLE with noise and Tweedie denoising. Figure 5: Guided MNIST samples from MLE-trained iTARFlow.

sections.heading: Appendix C Extended background on Boltzmann Generators
sections.text: Sampling from equilibrium distributions is a fundamental problem in statistical physics ( Frenkel and Smit, 1996 ; Tuckerman, 2023 ) , since equilibrium configurations provide access to thermodynamic observables and characterize the macroscopic behavior of physical systems ( Pathria, 2017 ) . For a configuration x x with energy ℰ ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{E}(x) at temperature T T , the equilibrium distribution is given by the Boltzmann distribution μ target ​ ( x ) = 1 𝒵 ​ exp ⁡ ( − β ​ ℰ ​ ( x ) ) , 𝒵 = ∫ exp ⁡ ( − β ​ ℰ ​ ( x ) ) ​ 𝑑 x , β = 1 k B ​ T , \mu_{\mathrm{target}}(x)=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\exp\left(-\beta\mathcal{E}(x)\right),\qquad\mathcal{Z}=\int\exp\left(-\beta\mathcal{E}(x)\right)\,dx,\qquad\beta=\frac{1}{k_{B}T}, (36) where 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} is the partition function, which is generally intractable for high-dimensional systems. A particularly important instance of this problem is the sampling of molecular configurations ( Zuckerman, 2011 ) . Equilibrium ensembles are required to characterize thermodynamic and conformational properties of molecular systems and are relevant to applications including biomolecular modeling and drug discovery ( Frenkel and Smit, 1996 ) . Sampling such systems is challenging because their energy landscapes are typically high-dimensional and multimodal, with metastable regions separated by large free-energy barriers. As a consequence, local sampling methods such as molecular dynamics (MD) ( Alder and Wainwright, 1959 ) and Markov chain Monte Carlo can exhibit long autocorrelation times and slow transitions between metastable states ( Wirnsberger et al., 2020 ; E et al., 2002 ) . Boltzmann Generators (BGs) ( Noé et al., 2019 ) address this challenge by learning a tractable generative model that approximates the target Boltzmann distribution. In particular, the model defines a distribution p θ ​ ( x ) p_{\theta}(x) such that p θ ​ ( x ) ≈ μ target ​ ( x ) , p^{\theta}(x)\approx\mu_{\mathrm{target}}(x), (37) while providing both a mechanism for efficiently drawing samples x ∼ p θ x\sim p^{\theta} and a tractable evaluation of their density p θ ​ ( x ) p^{\theta}(x) . The former enables direct generation of global proposals in configuration space, while the latter enables the use of Monte Carlo correction methods to account for discrepancies between the learned proposal distribution and the target distribution. One such correction is self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) ( Liu, 2001 ) . For an observable ϕ ⁡ ( x ) \phi(x) , its expectation under the target distribution can be written as 𝔼 μ target ​ [ ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ] = 𝔼 p θ ​ [ w ​ ( x ) ​ ϕ ​ ( x ) ] 𝔼 p θ ​ [ w ​ ( x ) ] , w ⁡ ( x ) = exp ⁡ ( − β ​ ℰ ​ ( x ) ) p θ ​ ( x ) . \mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\text{target}}}[\phi(x)]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p^{\theta}}\left[w(x)\phi(x)\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{p^{\theta}}\left[w(x)\right]},\qquad w(x)=\frac{\exp\left(-\beta\mathcal{E}(x)\right)}{p^{\theta}(x)}. (38) The unknown partition function 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} cancels in the ratio. Given K K independent samples x 1 , … , x K ∼ p θ x^{1},\ldots,x^{K}\sim p^{\theta} , the expectation can be approximated as 𝔼 μ target ​ [ ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ] ≈ ∑ i = 1 K w ¯ i ​ ϕ ​ ( x i ) , w ¯ i = w ⁡ ( x i ) ∑ j = 1 K w ⁡ ( x j ) . \mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\text{target}}}[\phi(x)]\approx\sum_{i=1}^{K}\bar{w}^{i}\phi(x_{i}),\qquad\bar{w}^{i}=\frac{w(x^{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}w(x^{j})}. (39) Beyond importance sampling, the learned model can also be combined with other Monte Carlo correction schemes. In particular, sequential Monte Carlo methods ( Tan et al., 2025a ) can use the generative model as a proposal while progressively bridging between the learned and target distributions through intermediate distributions and resampling steps. We refer to the appendix of ( Tan et al., 2025b ) for further discussion.

sections.heading: C.1 Baselines
sections.text: We compare NFM against a broad set of baselines covering both single-system and transferable molecular generative modeling. In the single-peptide setting, we include equivariant CNFs ( Klein et al., 2023b ; Klein and Noé, 2024 ) (ECNF++ ( Tan et al., 2025a ) ), RegFlow ( Rehman et al., 2026b ) , flow map based variants, FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) , F2D2 ( Ai et al., 2026 ) , and SCALLOP ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) . sections.heading: D.2 NFM Architecture
sections.text: Both NFM-D and NFM-R adopt modified versions of the iTARFlow architecture ( Lu et al., 2026b ) . NFM-D introduces time-conditioning via a sinusoidal timestep embedding module and injects this conditioning along with the class embedding into both the attention and the adaptive layernorm ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) modules within each block. NFM-R adapts iTARFlow to more closely follow the iMF architecture. The major changes are completely eliminating adaptive layer norm modules in favor of in-context conditioning and adopting general-purpose Transformer improvements: SwiGLU ( Shazeer, 2020 ) , RMSnorm ( Zhang and Sennrich, 2019 ) , RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) and QK-normalization. In-context conditioning . Following iMF we abandon adaLN-zero ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) in favor of in-context conditioning with multiple tokens for each condition. This change is particularly helpful given the need for our image models to condition on class, two timesteps and several CFG related conditions (c.f. § A.1 ), something which is better handled by introducing all conditioning into attention than simply summing their embeddings in an adaLN-zero module. Furthermore, adaLN-zero is known to be parameter-heavy ( Geng et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026b ) ; so this change potentially enables NFM-R to be more parameter efficient. Key to making in-context conditioning competitive with adaLN-zero is the use of multiple tokens per condition. Given a condition α ∈ ℝ \alpha\in\mathbb{R} , we jointly learn its embedding map g θ : ℝ ↦ ℝ n g_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{n} and m m embedding offsets { β i } i = 1 m , β i ∈ ℝ n \{\beta_{i}\}^{m}_{i=1},\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} . sections.heading: D.3.3 Numerical invertibility
sections.text: Noise annealing and FP64 inference . Theoretically, NFM-R should be exactly invertible; however, in practice, its regression objective combined with the denoiser parametrization can lead to a loss of numerical invertibility. As a mitigation strategy, we apply additive Gaussian noise to x 0 x_{0} before computing the interpolant and anneal its contribution to zero over the course of training (see § D.4 ). Through this strategy, it is possible to recover numerical invertibility in FP64 at inference. This strategy enabled the NFM-R CIFAR- 10 10 to be finetuned with REINFORCE to preferentially produce green frogs (§ E.1.1 ).

NFM s implement modified iTARFlow architectures (§ D.2 ). All model size configurations are based off the original iTARFlow and the NFM-R recipe follows pixel Mean Flow (pMF) ( Lu et al., 2026a ) . Following pMF, we use the Muon optimizer with Muon and AdamW weight decays of 0.1 and 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} respectively, and AdamW parameters ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) . For MLE iTARFlow we ablated the choice of optimizer Table 7 on CIFAR- 10 10 and used AdamW on both datasets. We train the MLE iTARFlow, NFM-D and noise annealed NFM-R CIFAR- 10 10 models for 960 epochs adopting a constant learning rate of 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} . The noise annealed NFM-R begins with σ = 0.5 \sigma=0.5 noise injected into the data, and this is annealed to 0 0 over the first 300 epochs. The numerically non-invertible NFM-R model follows a different training strategy; first we train solely with a flow matching loss (equivalently, only sampling s = t s=t in Algorithm 1 ) for 450 epochs at learning rate of 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} , next we resume training from EMA weights with the full iMF loss for 200 epochs with the same learning rate. This strategy is substantially cheaper and produces better samples. Similarly for ImageNet- 64 64 , NFM-R begins with flow matching training at a learning rate of 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} for 200 epochs, and resumes training with the full iMF loss for just 25 epochs at a lower learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} . On ImageNet- 64 64 both MLE iTARFlow and NFM-D train for 300 epochs with a linear warmup of 25 000 steps up to a learning rate of 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} . For NFM-D we found it beneficial to bring the learning rate down to 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} with a cosine decay from epoch 150 to 200, after the decay this learning rate is maintained until the end. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps ( NFM ), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFM s learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction. To enable scalable training of NFM s, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFM s that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process. On conditional image generation on CIFAR- 10 10 and ImageNet- 64 64 , NFM s achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFM s outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks. 1 Introduction Learning a transport map between a tractable reference distribution and the empirical distribution of complex data has become the de facto paradigm in generative modeling, with varied application domains spanning audiovisual media ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) , biomolecular modeling ( Abramson et al., 2024 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) , and scientific simulation ( Shu et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ) . Driving this widespread adoption is the ability to leverage standard alignment techniques such as best-of- N N selection ( Ramesh et al., 2021 ) , inference-time steering ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , and post-training algorithms ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) which effectively sharpen the model distribution—by increasing sample rewards assessed by an oracle. However, each generated sample necessitates computationally expensive numerical integration of an ODE or SDE—producing a substantial inference tax that computationally challenges the steering and post-training pipeline ( Wohlwend et al., 2025 ; Scarpellini et al., 2026 ) . Indeed, while typical Autoregressive LLMs have a mature post-training stack—e.g., PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , etc.—corresponding algorithmic frameworks for diffusion and flow model post-training are both vast and varied ( Wallace et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . The crucial distinction is that LLMs natively provide tractable sample likelihoods, whereas evaluating exact densities for diffusion and flow-matching models is computationally challenging. Specifically, evaluating sample likelihoods of flow models requires integrating the instantaneous change of variables along the underlying ODE, computing a high-dimensional network Jacobian, and necessitates stochastic trace estimation ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Meyer et al., 2021 ) . Instead, it is computationally more attractive to target the reward-tilted distribution, by modifying the drift of the underlying dynamics through path-space objectives. These objectives, however, crucially rely on high-variance value estimates of the terminal reward. More precisely, value function estimation necessitates propagating terminal rewards through noisy intermediate states, which requires backpropagating through time ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) –or a noisy single-step denoising approximation ( Blasingame and Liu, 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026b ) . These algorithmic features combine and give rise to tilting objectives that are inherently high variance, often leading to unstable post-training and mode collapse. Figure 1: Overview of NFM , which performs generative transport along a stochastic interpolant. NFM-R exploits pointwise matching at the particle level, while NFM-D leverages distributional matching. As generative models are deployed at scale, the cumulative cost of repeated sampling for generation, steering, and post-training makes inference efficiency a central design consideration. This practical motivation has led to the emergence of flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2025b ) , that directly learn the flow integrator , effectively compressing numerical simulation into few network evaluations. Although the exact ODE flow is a diffeomorphism, standard parameterizations are not invertible, nor do they provide tractable Jacobian determinants. While flow maps reduce the inference tax, they do not resolve the crucial likelihood-access gap—limiting their usage in scientific applications like Boltzmann Generators ( Noé et al., 2019 ) . As a result, classical Normalizing Flows (NF) ( Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010 ; Tabak and Turner, 2013 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ; Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ) trained with MLE remain an attractive exact likelihood-based model class. However, their practical deployment critically relies on noise injection into the clean data distribution for stable training, which unfortunately eliminates the promised access to cheap sample likelihood ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Taken together, these considerations motivate a new generative model that combines few-step sampling of flow maps with exact sample likelihoods for scalable, likelihood-based post-training. Current work . In this paper, we introduce Normalizing Flow Maps ( NFM ), a new generative model family, depicted in fig. 1 , that is purpose-built to deliver two objectives of interest: 1.) Exact sample likelihoods and 2.) Few-step inference ; thereby generalizing classical invertible normalizing flows and endowing flow maps with tractable likelihoods. An NFM defines a time-conditioned generative transport operator that is tied to the law of a known stochastic interpolant. However, unlike existing model classes, NFM by construction defines a family of tractable invertible maps connecting arbitrary points along a prescribed probability path. Consequently, NFM s provide exact sample likelihoods without expensive numerical integration. Importantly, restricting this family to the prior and data endpoints recovers a normalizing flow, and querying arbitrary time pairs yields the few-step transport characteristics of a flow map. As a result, NFM s are naturally suited for applications that require sample likelihoods, such as Boltzmann generators ( Noé et al., 2019 ) and RLHF post-training. To train NFM s, we operationalize two complementary matching principles inherent to NFM s, which in turn lead to self-distillation training objectives. In particular, our key insight is that NFM s must satisfy a known stochastic interpolant at a pointwise level and/or match its marginal distribution . The former condition unlocks regression-based training common in flow maps, but adapted to NFM , while the latter is an altogether new algorithmic framework that trains few-step generators by exploiting NFM s family of (end-point) invertible maps. We summarize our main contributions: 1. Model class . We introduce NFM , a new generative model class, that learns an invertible pushforward map, while natively supporting few-step sampling and exact sample likelihoods. 2. Training algorithms . Defined by matching principles (§ 3.2 ), we design two instantiations in NFM-R and NFM-D , which leverages pointwise and distributional matching respectively. In particular, NFM-R optimizes ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regression objectives. Meanwhile, NFM-D matches the induced pushforward distributions along the marginal law of the known forward process. 3. Empirical analysis . We evaluate NFM across image generation, post-training, and equilibrium sampling. On CIFAR- 10 10 and ImageNet- 64 64 , NFM improves over MLE-trained NFs in FID and FLD while for BGs NFM improves over prior continuous flow approaches.
